title: Design
summary: Design questions ask for a class whose operations meet a time target, often O(1). Pick one structure per job (a hash map to find, a list or queue to order) and keep them in sync on every operation.
idea: List the operations and their targets. Give each need its own structure: a map for lookup, a doubly linked list or deque for order. Update every structure in each operation.

signals.see: 'Implement a class with get and put in O(1)', or an LRU or LFU cache.
signals.think: A hash map finds the item; a doubly linked list keeps recency order and moves or removes a node in O(1).

signals.see: Allow at most k events per time window, or count hits in the last 5 minutes.
signals.think: Keep a queue of timestamps and drop the ones that slid out of the window, or use a token bucket that refills over time.

signals.see: Versioned values, snapshots or time-based lookups.
signals.think: Store a sorted list of (time, value) per key and binary-search it on read.

phrasings: Build a cache that evicts the least recently used item when it is full, with O(1) get and put.
Allow each user at most 3 requests in any 10-second window.
Store values by key and time, and return the value as of a given time.

picture.title: A plain list versus a map plus a doubly linked list
picture.alt: On the left, cache entries sit in an array in recency order, so finding a key or moving it to the front is a linear scan and shift. On the right, a hash map points from each key to its node in a doubly linked list; a hit unlinks the node and puts it at the front, and eviction removes the node before the tail, all in constant time.
picture.caption: The map finds the node; the list keeps the order. Update both.

input.ops: put 1 10, put 2 20, get 1, put 3 30, get 2, get 3

visualiser.inputHelp: A capacity from 1 to 3, and up to 8 operations like get 1 or put 1 10, separated by commas. Keys are 0 to 9 and values 0 to 99.

oneLiner: map key → node; doubly linked list in recency order; hit: unlink + to front; full: drop tail.prev

exercise.prompt: A limiter allows at most limit requests in any window of length window: a request at time t counts the allowed requests at times greater than t − window. times is sorted. Return, for each request, true if it is allowed. Rejected requests do not count. The starter never drops old requests from its log.
hints: Keep a queue of the times of allowed requests, oldest first.
Before deciding on time t, drop every logged time ≤ t − window: it has slid out of the window.
Allow the request if fewer than limit times remain, and log it. A rejected request is not logged.

complexity.why: The map finds a node in O(1) on average, and unlinking or inserting a node in a doubly linked list changes a fixed number of pointers. The cache never holds more than capacity nodes.

mistakes: Using a singly linked list, so removing a node needs its predecessor and a scan.
Updating the list but not the map (or the other way round) on eviction or overwrite.
Forgetting that put on an existing key also makes it the most recent.
Skipping sentinel head and tail nodes, then special-casing an empty list or the first node.

quiz.question: Why does an LRU cache need a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?
choices: To unlink any node in O(1), which needs its previous node
quiz.explain: With prev pointers, a node found through the map can be removed without a scan.

quiz.question: What do the sentinel head and tail nodes buy you?
choices: Every real node always has a prev and a next, so insert and unlink need no special cases
quiz.explain: The list is never truly empty, so the edge cases disappear.

quiz.question: A sliding-log rate limiter keeps request times in a queue. When is a time removed?
choices: When it falls out of the window, before deciding on the new request
quiz.explain: Only times inside the window count against the limit.

interviewTip: List the operations and their time targets first, then name a structure for each need. Interviewers look for the moment you say 'the map finds it, the list orders it'.
